Guideline
Subject: Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR)
Chapter 1 – Overview of risk-based capital requirements
1.3 Effective Date
This policy on Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR) becomes effective in November 2023 for institutions with a fiscal year ending October 31, and in January 2024 for institutions with a fiscal year ending December 31.
Note: For institutions with a fiscal year ending October 31 or November 30, respectively.
3.1 General Principles
This policy outlines the capital adequacy requirements for banks (including federal credit unions), bank holding companies, federally regulated trust companies, and federally regulated loan companies, collectively referred to as 'institutions'. The key principles of this policy are:

- Institutions must maintain adequate capital in accordance with the Bank Act and Trust and Loan Companies Act.
- The capital standards in this guideline, along with the leverage requirements, provide the framework for the Superintendent to assess the capital adequacy of institutions.
- The Superintendent has established two minimum standards: a leverage ratio and a risk-based capital ratio. These measures assess the overall adequacy of an institution's capital and the risks faced by the institution.
- The Superintendent retains the authority to direct an institution to increase its capital, even if it meets the minimum standards.
4.1 Management Responsibilities
OSFI, as the regulatory authority, is responsible for developing and maintaining this Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR) guideline. OSFI, as a member of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, participated in the development of the Basel capital framework on which this guideline is based. OSFI is also responsible for assessing the capital adequacy of institutions and directing them to increase capital as necessary.

4.2 Institutional Responsibilities
Institutions subject to this policy, including banks (including federal credit unions), bank holding companies, federally regulated trust companies, and federally regulated loan companies, are responsible for maintaining adequate capital in accordance with the requirements outlined in this guideline. Where relevant, the Basel framework paragraph numbers are provided in square brackets at the end of each paragraph referencing material from the Basel framework.
5.1 Implementation Procedures
OSFI will monitor institutions' compliance with the capital adequacy requirements outlined in this guideline on an ongoing basis. Institutions are required to submit regular reporting to OSFI to demonstrate their adherence to the capital standards.

5.2 Control Mechanisms
In addition to the capital adequacy requirements in this guideline, domestic systemically important banks are also subject to the Total Loss Absorbing Capacity (TLAC) requirements described in a separate OSFI guideline. OSFI will utilize various control mechanisms, such as on-site inspections and targeted reviews, to validate the effectiveness of institutions' capital management practices.

6.1 Compliance Requirements
Institutions must comply with the capital adequacy requirements set forth in this guideline. Failure to maintain adequate capital levels may result in regulatory actions, as described in section 6.3.

6.2 Monitoring and Review
OSFI will regularly review this Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR) guideline to ensure it remains current and aligned with evolving regulatory standards. OSFI may update the guideline as needed, and institutions will be notified of any changes.
1.1 Purpose and Scope

This chapter provides an overview of the risk-based capital requirements for banks (including federal credit unions), bank holding companies, federally regulated trust companies, and federally regulated loan companies, collectively referred to as 'institutions'. These capital adequacy requirements are set out in the Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR) guideline, which consists of nine chapters that should be read in conjunction with each other.
1.2 Scope
This Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR) guideline consists of nine chapters that collectively set out the requirements for banks (including federal credit unions), bank holding companies, federally regulated trust companies, and federally regulated loan companies. The chapters are as follows:

1. Overview of Risk-based Capital Requirements
2. Definition of Capital
3. Operational Risk
4. Credit Risk - Standardized Approach
5. Credit Risk - Internal Ratings-Based Approach
6. Securitization
7. Settlement and Counterparty Risk
8. Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Risk
9. Market Risk

This document should be read in conjunction with the other CAR chapters to ensure a comprehensive understanding of the capital adequacy requirements.

Chapter 1 – Overview of Risk-based Capital Requirements
1.1 Purpose
This chapter provides an overview of the capital adequacy requirements for banks (including federal credit unions), bank holding companies, federally regulated trust companies, and federally regulated loan companies, collectively referred to as 'institutions'.
1.2 Scope
This chapter is drawn from the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) Basel Framework published on the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) website. The Basel paragraph numbers associated with the text in this chapter are indicated in square brackets at the end of each paragraph.
1.3 Effective Date
November 2023 / January 2024

Note: For institutions with a fiscal year ending October 31 or December 31, respectively.
3.1 General Principles
The capital adequacy requirements outlined in this guideline apply on a consolidated basis to the following institutions:
  a. All institutions designated by OSFI as domestic systemically important banks (D-SIBs)
  b. Small and medium-sized deposit-taking institutions (SMSBs), which fall into Categories I, II or III as defined in OSFI's SMSB Capital and Liquidity Requirements Guideline
3.1 General Principles
The consolidated entity includes all subsidiaries except insurance subsidiaries. Institutions are expected to hold capital within the consolidated group in a manner that is consistent with the level and location of risk.
2. Definitions

Tier 1 capital: Consists of Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital and Additional Tier 1 capital.

Tier 2 capital: One of the elements that makes up total capital.
2. Definitions

Total capital: The sum of Tier 1 capital and Tier 2 capital.


2. Definitions

SMSB (Small and medium-sized deposit-taking institutions): Banks (including federal credit unions), bank holding companies, federally regulated trust companies, and federally regulated loan companies that have not been designated by OSFI as domestic systemically important banks (D-SIBs). This includes subsidiaries of SMSBs or D-SIBs that are banks (including federal credit unions), federally regulated trust companies or federally regulated loan companies.

The criteria for the capital elements comprising the two tiers, as well as the various limits, restrictions and regulatory adjustments to which they are subject, are described in Chapter 2.
Total Risk-weighted Assets
Risk-weighted assets (RWA) make up the denominator of the risk-based capital ratios, and is calculated as the higher of:
a. the sum of the following three elements:
  i. RWA for credit risk;
  ii. RWA for market risk; and 
  iii. RWA for operational risk; and
b. the adjusted RWA determined as per the capital floor described in section 1.5.
[Basel Framework, RBC 20.4]
Credit Risk
RWA for credit risk (including counterparty credit risk) is calculated as the sum of:
a. Credit RWA for banking book exposures which, except the RWA listed in (b) through (e) below, is calculated using:
  i. the standardized approach (as set out in Chapter 4); or
  ii. the Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) approach (as set out in Chapter 5).
b. RWA for counterparty credit risk from banking book exposures and trading book exposures (as set out in Chapter 7), except the exposures listed in (c) and (f) below.
c. Credit RWA for equity investments in funds that are held in the banking book calculated using one or more of the approaches set out in Chapter 4:
  i. The look-through approach
  ii. The mandate-based approach
  iii. The fall-back approach
d. RWA for securitization exposures held in the banking book, calculating using one or more of the approaches set out in Chapter 6:
  i. Securitization Standardized Approach (SEC-SA)
  ii. Securitization External Ratings-Based Approach (SEC-ERBA)
  iii. Securitization Internal Ratings-Based Approach (SEC-IRBA)
  iv. Securitization Internal Assessment Approach (SEC-IAA)
  v. A risk weight of 1250% in cases where the institution cannot use (i) to (iv) above.
